text: Are the stereotypes about women true? Number one, women are bad drivers. Statistically, men are actually much worse drivers. So bad that their insurance rates are actually higher than ours. They cause more accidents, they get more traffic tickets, and they have more DUIs than women. When she alludes to women being better drivers, she probably means safer drivers. Because better is a vague term and can mean different things. But even with safer, there are nuances. Yes, men are involved in more accidents and especially more fatal crashes than women. But men on average also drive more miles or kilometers. So to be precise, we need to look at data per mile or per kilometer driven. In fact, one of the most cited studies in this topic, a peer-reviewed paper called Vulnerability of Female Drivers in Motor Vehicle Crashes, showed that women actually have higher crash involvement per mile driven. But there's an important nuance. When it comes to fatal crashes per mile, men still show higher numbers. And if you judge better drivers in a more sports sense, like Formula One, NASCAR, and so on, there is no gender restriction for participating, but the vast majority of drivers are still men. So again, the question of who are better drivers, men or women, is quite nuanced and depends a lot on the criteria you use. Number two, women talk too much. Studies show that men actually talk more. Not just one, multiple studies across many different contexts, like school and work, have concluded that it is in fact true. Men talk more, but perceive that they have talked less. We all know that men are known to interrupt women, talk over us, silence us, and make our ideas. And now it's even shown in studies. It would actually be nice to see what studies she's referring to. Because there is a very famous study by Matthias Mell, published in Science in 2007, which was specifically aimed at testing the stereotype that women talk more. He tracked real conversations using audio snippets and found that women spoke around 16,215 words per day, while men spoke around 15,669 words per day. So yes, women did speak slightly more, but the difference was not statistically significant. In other words, men and women tend to speak roughly the same amount. So I'm not sure where her claim that men talk more is coming from. What is generally observed though, is that women tend to communicate in a more interactive back and forth way, while men are more likely to speak in a monologue style. Number three, my personal favorite. Men are better leaders than women. According to Dr. Amen, a famous brain specialist who has studied over 250,000 brains. After comparing male versus female brains, not only does he say that we are completely different species, but that women's brains are not only superior, we are literally wired for leadership. Science is so hot. Yes, science is hot, especially when it's used properly. She's most likely referring to Daniel Amen, an American psychiatrist. And I can tell you right away, if a scientist says that men and women are completely different species, that should immediately raise questions about that scientist's credibility. And yes, this doctor is widely criticized within the scientific community. What mainstream science actually shows is that male and female brains do have small average differences, but there is a huge overlap. And the bigger question is, how do those differences translate into leadership ability? In reality, there is no strong body of evidence showing that men or women are inherently better leaders. It is almost like leadership could depend much more on the individual rather than on gender.
